2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern for aggregate INEGI census cross-sections (1990, 2005, 2010), which enumerate full municipal populations rather than a longitudinal cohort; however, severe post-2003 administrative reporting attrition occurred as SACM curtailed public disclosure of metering, customer-registry, and contract performance metrics (PDF p. 12 / p. 685).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Table 3 presents unadjusted census connection percentages across the DF, Outer ZMCM, Outer ZMVM, and Mexico with no statistical control for major confounders explicitly acknowledged in the text, including starkly different population growth rates (5% in DF vs. 52% in Outer ZMCM and 57% in Outer ZMVM), baseline ceiling effects in DF, different water-official tenure lengths (6-year vs. 3-year terms), urban in-migration, and aquifer depletion (PDF pp. 8-9 / pp. 681-682).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-weak: The study clearly delineates the 1994 four-zone private service/concession structure (Tables 1, 2, and 4), the institutional transition from CADF (1992) to SACM (2003), municipal tenure rules, and civil-society appeals under the 2002 Federal Transparency Law of Access to Public Information, but relies on secondary literature, press reports, and personal communications rather than primary contract texts, municipal decrees, or regulatory filings (partly due to SACM opacity post-2003).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Household access rates in Table 3 use standardized INEGI census categories (basic network access vs. in-home piped connection), though basic access conflates standpipes and piped supply; post-2003 contract performance, efficiency stagnation, and political 'disinformation' claims rely on secondary reports, news articles, corporate press releases, and informal correspondence without standardized measurement instruments (PDF pp. 5, 8, 11-13 / pp. 678, 681, 684-686).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Mixed: Aggregate household connection coverage is measured via national census waves (1990, 2005, 2010) held to consistent pre-2004 SEDESOL metropolitan boundaries (PDF pp. 5-6, 8 / pp. 678-679, 681), but census access indicators omit water quality, intermittency, pressure, and affordability, while post-2003 operational and equity outcomes rely on qualitative summaries of secondary audits (UNAM 2010) and media reports of rationing cutoffs.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No study protocol or pre-analysis plan exists; census comparisons report 1990, 2005, and 2010 while omitting 1995 and 2000 INEGI waves without explanation, and the Abstract and Conclusions assert unequivocally that privatization 'clearly improved the quality of the city's physical infrastructure and service provision' (PDF p. 14 / p. 687) despite earlier acknowledging that 'it is not entirely clear whether the improvements are attributable to service privatization' (PDF p. 9 / p. 682).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Documentary sources, news reports, corporate circulars, and the three personal-communication informants (SACM director, Suez/Bal-Ondeo representative, UNAM researcher; PDF p. 12 / p. 685) were purposively selected with no documented search strategy, inclusion criteria, or informant recruitment protocol, creating substantial risk of selective source inclusion for the opaque post-2003 period.

domain_ratings.justification: Administrative milestones—such as the 1992 creation of CADF, the 1994 10-year four-zone service contracts, the 2003 merger of DGCOH and CADF into SACM, post-2003 contract extensions, and COMDA's 2011 administrative appeal under the 2002 Federal Transparency Law of Access to Public Information—are coherently traced using academic audits (UNAM 2010; Tortajada 2006) and official bulletins. However, primary legal instruments, statutory citations, and actual concession contracts are never directly cited (partly due to SACM non-disclosure), and Table 1 conflates task-based service contracts with concession contracts.

The paper rigorously distinguishes nested administrative and hydrological jurisdictions: the Federal District (DF) and its 16 boroughs partitioned into 4 concession zones (Tables 2 and 4), the Outer ZMCM (16 State of Mexico municipalities), the Outer ZMVM, and federal jurisdiction (CONAGUA). It also explicitly accounts for the 2004 SEDESOL metropolitan boundary redefinition by holding pre-2004 boundaries constant for longitudinal comparability and notes differences in institutional tenure (6-year DF utility terms vs. 3-year surrounding municipal terms).

The institutional exposure—Mexico City's decentralized four-zone private water service partnership model (1994-2003 initial term under CADF with a three-part mandate covering infrastructure efficiency, customer registry/metering, and revenue collection, followed by post-2003 renewals and consortium restructurings under SACM)—is clearly mapped by zone, consortium partners, and constituent boroughs. However, post-2003 contractual obligations, tariff formulas, and remuneration terms remain vague because contract renegotiations were shielded from public disclosure.

In Table 3, quantitative access outcomes distinguish 'Basic access' (general connection to formal water networks including standpipes and piped supply) from 'In-home piped connection' based on INEGI census classifications, and the author explicitly flags that network connection counts mask service quality and intermittency. Operational and governance outcomes (metering expansion, revenue collection, registry backlogs, public transparency) are defined narratively via secondary evaluations (Tortajada 2006; UNAM 2010).

While Table 3 uses full-population aggregate Mexican census tabulations (1990, 2005, 2010), the study reports no literature search strategy, documentary sampling frame, or respondent recruitment design for its qualitative/historical evidence, including the three 'personal communication' contacts cited on p. 685 (an SACM director, a Suez/Bal-Ondeo representative, and a UNAM researcher).

Inclusion of secondary articles, corporate press releases, news reports, civil-society bulletins, and personal communications is entirely purposive and undocumented, with no criteria to guard against selective source inclusion—especially for the post-2003 period where verifiable public records were scarce and no community or poor-borough informants were directly consulted.

Geographic aggregation rules and exclusions for Table 3 (Outer ZMCM excluding DF; Outer ZMVM excluding ZMCM) and data sources (INEGI 2010; SEDESOL 2004) are transparently documented, though 20-year growth figures are presented as relative percentage growth without explicit formula notes and intermediate census waves (1995, 2000) are omitted. Post-2003 operational stagnation and political motivation claims rely on unstandardized narrative reports rather than systematic indicators.

Empirical comparisons rely solely on unadjusted three-period aggregate census tabulations and historical process tracing without a statistical counterfactual or quasi-experimental design. Although the author candidly states on p. 682 that 'it is not entirely clear whether the improvements are attributable to service privatization,' the Abstract and Conclusions overstate causal attribution by asserting that privatization 'clearly improved' infrastructure quality, efficiency, and financial stability.

Major confounding differences between the DF and surrounding metropolitan zones—including dramatic differences in 20-year population growth (5% in DF vs. 52% in Outer ZMCM and 57% in Outer ZMVM), higher baseline connection levels in DF, longer utility-official tenure in DF (6 years vs. 3 years), urban in-migration, and political/fiscal capacity—are discussed qualitatively as caveats on pp. 681-682, but no analytical adjustment or borough-level disaggregation is performed.

The study provides rich, multi-scalar political-economy contextualization linking pre-1997 appointed PRI governance, post-1997 PRD electoral dominance and presidential ambitions (Cárdenas, López Obrador, Encinas, Ebrard), multinational corporate exits and consolidations (Veolia, Severn Trent, United Utilities, Suez/Bal-Ondeo), federal-municipal partisan conflict (PAN/CONAGUA vs. PRD/SACM), and COMDA's formal transparency mobilization.

While the aggregate INEGI census comparisons in Table 3 could be approximately replicated using 1990, 2005, and 2010 census releases and pre-2004 SEDESOL metropolitan definitions, key post-2003 institutional claims depend on unpublished October 2010 personal communications, transient web/news URLs, and an undocumented source-selection process.

No documentary coding protocol, content-analysis framework, or structured interview/correspondence instrument is reported for synthesizing press releases, media coverage, evaluation reports, or personal communications.

Beyond standard funding and collegial acknowledgements (p. 688), the author provides no discussion of researcher positionality, how insider access to SACM and Suez/Bal-Ondeo officials shaped interpretations, or potential evaluative bias when attributing ulterior partisan motives ('disinformation campaign') to municipal actors.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment; no numeric composite score), Pierce (2012) is a single-city political-economy and institutional-historical case study of water service privatization contracts in Mexico City (Distrito Federal, 1994-2011), supplemented by unadjusted aggregate INEGI census tabulations (1990, 2005, 2010) and three informal stakeholder communications. Methodological strengths lie in jurisdictional specificity (D2: strong) and multi-scalar institutional contextualization (D10: strong): the author carefully distinguishes the DF's 16 boroughs and 4 concession zones from surrounding State of Mexico metropolitan rings (Outer ZMCM and Outer ZMVM) while holding pre-2004 SEDESOL boundaries constant, and traces municipal-federal partisan dynamics (PRI, PRD, PAN), consortium restructurings, and COMDA's invocation of the 2002 Federal Transparency Law. Legal source accuracy (D1), exposure definition (D3), outcome definition (D4), and measurement transparency (D7) are adequate, though constrained by reliance on secondary literature and press reports rather than primary concession contracts or statutory texts (compounded by SACM's post-2003 secrecy). Conversely, sampling transparency (D5), source/informant selection (D6), causal identification (D8), treatment of confounding (D9), replication potential (D11), coding transparency (D12), and researcher reflexivity (D13) are weak. In particular, Table 3 compares aggregate connection rates across zones experiencing vastly different 20-year population growth (5% in DF vs. 52% in Outer ZMCM and 57% in Outer ZMVM) without statistical adjustment, and the Conclusions overstate causal attribution regarding efficiency and infrastructure improvements despite the text's earlier admission on p. 682 that causal attribution to privatization is unclear.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (strong jurisdictional and institutional contextualization, adequate exposure/outcome description, weak sampling/coding transparency and weak causal/confounding control)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Single-city political-economy and legal-institutional historical case study of municipal water service privatization contracts (1994-2011), supplemented by descriptive aggregate census tabulations (1990, 2005, 2010) and informal stakeholder correspondence
raw_response.where_found_summary: Data and Methodology (PDF p. 5 / p. 678); Before Service Privatization & Privatization Structure (PDF pp. 5-7 / pp. 678-680, Tables 1-2); Impact of Service Privatization on Household Water Access (PDF pp. 7-9 / pp. 680-682, Table 3); Political Economy & Post-2003 Contract Renegotiations / Transparency Sections (PDF pp. 9-14 / pp. 682-687, Table 4); Conclusions & Notes (PDF pp. 14-15 / pp. 687-688).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Pierce (2012) is an institutional and political-economy historical case study analyzing municipal water concession/service governance, administrative restructuring (CADF to SACM), post-2003 contract renegotiation opacity, and transparency-law mobilization in Mexico City, accompanied only by a five-row descriptive summary table of aggregate INEGI census percentages (Table 3) and three cited personal communications. It is not a quasi-experimental comparative evaluation with statistical counterfactual estimation (ruling out ROBINS-I, which excludes descriptive single-case histories without econometric comparator analysis), not a unit-level analytical cross-sectional or cohort study (ruling out JBI checklists), not a primary qualitative interview/ethnographic study with participant recruitment and qualitative coding or a genuine primary mixed-methods design (ruling out CASP and MMAT), and not a systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly fits this institutional/legal-historical case study design.
